lessons.title: Building a stable pallet
lessons.html:
What is palletising?

Palletising means stacking packed cartons onto a pallet in a fixed pattern, so they can be moved by forklift, cooled, stored and shipped as one unit. A good pallet is straight, stable and strong, and lets cold air flow through the cartons.

Before you start

  • Check the pallet instruction: market, carton type, number of cartons per layer, number of layers and the stacking pattern.
  • Use only the correct pallet type. Check it is clean and dry, with no broken planks or loose nails. Export pallets may need to be heat-treated and marked.
  • Place the pallet base square on the floor or on the palletising station.

Stacking

  1. Place the first layer exactly in the pattern on the instruction. The cartons must be in line with the edges of the pallet, not hanging over, and not too far inside.
  2. Keep all cartons in the same direction as shown, with labels facing outwards where required.
  3. Stack each layer straight on top of the one below so that carton corners and walls line up. The strength of a carton is in its corners.
  4. Keep the ventilation holes of the cartons lined up so cold air can flow through.
  5. Do not mix different cultivars, grades, counts or markets on one pallet unless the instruction says it is a mixed pallet.
  6. Count the cartons as you go and stop at the correct number of layers.

Handle cartons carefully

Do not throw, drop or stand on cartons. Lift with your legs, keep your back straight and hold the carton close to your body. Do not lift above shoulder height without a step. Damaged cartons must be repacked, not hidden in the middle of the pallet.

lessons.title: Strapping, labelling and moving pallets
lessons.html:
Securing the pallet

A finished pallet must not move or lean during transport. It is held together with:

  • Corner boards (angle boards) on all four corners, from the bottom to the top layer.
  • Straps placed at the levels set in the instruction, pulled tight with the strapping machine or tool, but not so tight that they crush the cartons.
  • Sometimes a top sheet or cap and net or stretch wrap, depending on the market.

Check the pallet from all sides. It should be straight up and down, with no bulging cartons and no gaps.

Pallet card and labels

Each pallet gets a pallet card or barcode label. It shows a pallet number and information such as the producer, packhouse, cultivar, grade, count, number of cartons and packing date. This is linked to traceability and export documents. Check that the information on the card matches the cartons on the pallet. Put the label on the side and position the instruction says.

Records

Write down or scan the pallet number, the number of cartons and the time it was finished. Report any pallet that has damaged cartons or is short of cartons.

Moving the pallet

  • Pallets are moved by trained forklift drivers or with a pallet jack by trained workers.
  • Move finished pallets to the cold room quickly. Fruit must not wait in the warm packing hall.
  • Never stand under a raised load or walk in the forklift lane.
  • Do not ride on pallet jacks or forklifts.

Strapping safety

Straps can whip back when cut or when they break. Cut straps holding the strap end, standing to the side, and wear safety glasses if required. Keep fingers out of the strapping machine.

Key points

  • Follow the pallet instruction for pattern, cartons per layer and layers.
  • Stack cartons straight, corner on corner, with vents lined up.
  • Do not mix cultivars, grades or counts unless it is a mixed pallet.
  • Use corner boards and straps, and attach the correct pallet card.
  • Move finished pallets to cold storage quickly and safely.
